Complete means two things: mutually commuting, and enough of them that every eigenspace has been cut down to a single line, so the labels determine the state uniquely. When you write the hydrogen states as ∣n,ℓ,m⟩\ket{n,\ell,m}∣n,ℓ,m⟩ you are naming the eigenvalues of three commuting operators. And the reason the labels are consistent, which is to say the reason a state can have a definite ℓ\ellℓ and a definite mmm at the same time, is Step 4 above, and nothing else.

Run it backwards and you get the other half. If [A,B]≠0[A,B]\neq0[A,B]=0 there is no common eigenbasis, so there is no state in which both observables are sharp. That is the qualitative content of Chapter 4.9. The quantitative version is the Cauchy–Schwarz bound ΔA ΔB≥12∣⟨[A,B]⟩∣\Delta A\,\Delta B\ge\tfrac12\abs{\avg{[A,B]}}ΔAΔB≥21​∣⟨[A,B]⟩∣ from §1, whose right-hand side is non-zero exactly when the operators fail to commute. The two great mysteries of quantum mechanics, why can some quantities be known together and others not?, are one theorem about matrices, proved above, with an "if and only if" in the middle.

Familiar ground

You have run principal component analysis on expression data, on imaging features, on multiplexed assay panels. Here is what was actually happening, and why it could not have failed.

Centre the data matrix XXX (nnn samples ×\times× ppp features) and form the covariance matrix Σ=1n−1X ⁣⊤ ⁣X\Sigma = \tfrac{1}{n-1}X^{\!\top}\!XΣ=n−11​X⊤X, whose entries are Σij=cov(feature i,feature j)\Sigma_{ij}=\mathrm{cov}(\text{feature }i,\text{feature }j)Σij​=cov(feature i,feature j). Covariance is symmetric in its two arguments, so Σ ⁣⊤=Σ\Sigma^{\!\top}=\SigmaΣ⊤=Σ. A real covariance matrix is Hermitian by construction, not by assumption and not by luck. Section 6 therefore guarantees, as a theorem:

  • The eigenvalues are real. They are variances, so this had better be true. It is not a numerical accident, and it does not depend on the data.
  • The principal components are mutually orthogonal. Uncorrelated components are not something PCA arranges by cleverness. They come out perpendicular because §6(b) says eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix with distinct eigenvalues have no choice.
  • They span the whole feature space. Completeness (0.5.21) says no direction of variation is missed, so reconstructing from all ppp components returns your data exactly.

More is true, and it is worth being precise about the extra. Σ\SigmaΣ is not merely Hermitian. It is positive semi-definite, and one line shows it for any direction uuu:

u ⁣⊤Σu=1n−1∥Xu∥2  ≥  0, u^{\!\top}\Sigma u = \tfrac{1}{n-1}\left\lVert Xu\right\rVert^{2} \;\ge\; 0, u⊤Σu=n−11​∥Xu∥2≥0,

because it is a sum of squares, and that sum is exactly the sample variance of the data projected onto uuu. Apply this to a unit eigenvector and it gives λ=u ⁣⊤Σu≥0\lambda = u^{\!\top}\Sigma u\ge0λ=u⊤Σu≥0. So the eigenvalues are not just real, they are non-negative, and each eigenvalue is the variance along its own component. Positive semi-definiteness is strictly stronger than Hermiticity: a Hermitian matrix may have negative eigenvalues, and a covariance matrix may not.

Two further standard facts now cost one line each. Write a unit vector as u=∑iciuiu=\sum_i c_iu_iu=∑i​ci​ui​ in the eigenbasis with ∑ici2=1\sum_i c_i^{2}=1∑i​ci2​=1. The spectral decomposition then gives u ⁣⊤Σu=∑iλici2u^{\!\top}\Sigma u=\sum_i\lambda_ic_i^{2}u⊤Σu=∑i​λi​ci2​, a weighted average of the eigenvalues, and a weighted average is maximised by putting all the weight on the largest. The first principal component is the top eigenvector because a weighted average is largest when it is not an average. And by (0.5.45) the total variance is tr⁡Σ=∑iλi\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=\sum_i\lambda_itrΣ=∑i​λi​, which is why "proportion of variance explained" is λi/∑jλj\lambda_i/\sum_j\lambda_jλi​/∑j​λj​ and why those fractions sum to one.

Now the point worth carrying away. PCA works for exactly the same reason quantum measurement outcomes are real numbers. One theorem, §6, applied twice. Once to a covariance matrix, where the real eigenvalues are variances and the orthogonal eigenvectors are uncorrelated components. Once to a Hamiltonian, where the real eigenvalues are energies and the orthogonal eigenvectors are distinguishable states. It is not an analogy and not a coincidence of formalism. It is one theorem with two costumes, and you have been using the harder-looking costume for years without noticing.

In plain terms 0.5.8

Two maps of the self-partnered kind fall apart into the same independent directions when, and only when, the order of applying them makes no difference. Half of that is easy: if both are lists of numbers over one shared set of directions, then numbers commute and so must the maps. The other half carries the content. Wherever the first map cannot distinguish between several directions, having given them all the same number, the second goes inside that ambiguity and chooses, and between them they produce one set of directions suiting both.

This is how a physical state comes to be labelled by a handful of numbers, one from each map, the labels fixing the state completely once there are enough maps to leave no ambiguity. The reason such labels can coexist, which is to say the reason a state may have a definite value of one quantity and simultaneously of another, is the argument above and nothing besides.

Run it backwards for the other half. Where two maps fail to commute there is no shared set of directions, so no state exists in which both quantities are sharp, and the size of the failure is what the overlap inequality from the opening of the chapter measures. The two things people find most mysterious about quantum mechanics are one theorem about matrices with an if and only if in it.

9 · Worked examples

Worked example 1 — the two-state system, diagonalised completely

Take the Hermitian matrix

H=(E0ΔΔE0),E0,Δ∈R, Δ>0. H = \begin{pmatrix}E_0 & \Delta\\ \Delta & E_0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad E_0,\Delta\in\R,\ \Delta\gt0. H=(E0​Δ​ΔE0​​),E0​,Δ∈R, Δ>0.

It is real and symmetric, hence Hermitian, so §6 applies before we compute anything. The eigenvalues will be real and the eigenvectors perpendicular. Let us watch it happen.

Eigenvalues. From (0.5.34),

det⁡(E0−λΔΔE0−λ)=(E0−λ)2−Δ2=0, \det\begin{pmatrix}E_0-\lambda & \Delta\\ \Delta & E_0-\lambda\end{pmatrix} = (E_0-\lambda)^{2}-\Delta^{2} = 0, det(E0​−λΔ​ΔE0​−λ​)=(E0​−λ)2−Δ2=0,

and that is a difference of two squares, so take square roots of both sides:

⟹E0−λ=±Δ⟹λ±=E0±Δ. \Longrightarrow\quad E_0-\lambda = \pm\Delta \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda_{\pm} = E_0\pm\Delta. ⟹E0​−λ=±Δ⟹λ±​=E0​±Δ.

Real, as promised. And note what has happened here. A matrix with equal diagonal entries, two "levels" of the same value E0E_0E0​, has eigenvalues that are split apart by the off-diagonal coupling, into E0+ΔE_0+\DeltaE0​+Δ and E0−ΔE_0-\DeltaE0​−Δ, separated by 2Δ2\Delta2Δ.

Eigenvectors. For λ+=E0+Δ\lambda_{+}=E_0+\Deltaλ+​=E0​+Δ, solve (H−λ+I)v=0(H-\lambda_{+}I)v=0(H−λ+​I)v=0:

(−ΔΔΔ−Δ)(v1v2)=0  ⟹  v1=v2  ⟹  ∣+⟩=12(11). \begin{pmatrix}-\Delta & \Delta\\ \Delta & -\Delta\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}v_1\\v_2\end{pmatrix}=0 \;\Longrightarrow\; v_1=v_2 \;\Longrightarrow\; \ket{+}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}. (−ΔΔ​Δ−Δ​)(v1​v2​​)=0⟹v1​=v2​⟹∣+⟩=2​1​(11​).

For λ−=E0−Δ\lambda_{-}=E_0-\Deltaλ−​=E0​−Δ the matrix becomes (ΔΔΔΔ)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\Delta&\Delta\\\Delta&\Delta\end{smallmatrix}\right)(ΔΔ​ΔΔ​), forcing v1=−v2v_1=-v_2v1​=−v2​, so ∣−⟩=12(1−1)\ket{-}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}∣−⟩=2​1​(1−1​). Both have been normalised by dividing by 12+12\sqrt{1^{2}+1^{2}}12+12​.

Orthogonality, checked. ⟨+∣−⟩=12(1⋅1+1⋅(−1))=0.\avg{+|-} = \tfrac12\big(1\cdot1 + 1\cdot(-1)\big) = 0.⟨+∣−⟩=21​(1⋅1+1⋅(−1))=0. ✓ Perpendicular, exactly as §6(b) requires. We never used that fact to find them, so this is a genuine test rather than a restatement.

Spectral decomposition. Build the projections P±=∣±⟩⟨±∣P_{\pm}=\ket{\pm}\bra{\pm}P±​=∣±⟩⟨±∣ as column times row:

P+=12(11)(11)=12(1111),P−=12(1−1−11). P_{+} = \tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\end{pmatrix} = \tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad P_{-} = \tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}. P+​=21​(11​)(1​1​)=21​(11​11​),P−​=21​(1−1​−11​).

Sanity checks: P++P−=IP_{+}+P_{-}=IP+​+P−​=I ✓ (completeness), P+P−=0P_{+}P_{-}=0P+​P−​=0 ✓ (orthogonality), P±2=P±P_{\pm}^{2}=P_{\pm}P±2​=P±​ ✓ (idempotence).

Reconstruction. Now rebuild HHH from its spectrum alone, which is the claim of §6.3 made concrete:

λ+P++λ−P−=E0+Δ2(1111)+E0−Δ2(1−1−11)=(E0ΔΔE0)  =  H.  ✓ \begin{aligned} \lambda_{+}P_{+}+\lambda_{-}P_{-} &= \tfrac{E_0+\Delta}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix} + \tfrac{E_0-\Delta}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}\\[6pt] &= \begin{pmatrix}E_0 & \Delta\\ \Delta & E_0\end{pmatrix} \;=\; H. \;\checkmark \end{aligned} λ+​P+​+λ−​P−​​=2E0​+Δ​(11​11​)+2E0​−Δ​(1−1​−11​)=(E0​Δ​ΔE0​​)=H.✓​

The matrix has been completely dissolved into two numbers and two perpendicular directions, and reassembled from them.

Why this example and not another. The eigenvalues E0±ΔE_0\pm\DeltaE0​±Δ are a level splitting. Two states that would be degenerate at energy E0E_0E0​ are pushed apart by the coupling Δ\DeltaΔ, and the new eigenstates are the symmetric and antisymmetric combinations rather than either original state. This 2×22\times22×2 matrix is the most reused object in all of quantum mechanics. It is the ammonia molecule, whose two mirror-image configurations split by 2Δ2\Delta2Δ and give the ammonia maser. It is neutrino oscillation, where the states of definite mass are not the states of definite flavour and the mismatch makes them convert into one another. It is the qubit, where ∣+⟩\ket{+}∣+⟩ and ∣−⟩\ket{-}∣−⟩ are the two states you engineer and control. Chapter 4.2 will do all three, and the linear algebra will already be finished.

Worked example 2 — eiθσx\ee^{\ii\theta\sigma_x}eiθσx​, or Euler's formula with a matrix in the exponent

Let

σx=(0110), \sigma_x = \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}, σx​=(01​10​),

which is real symmetric, hence Hermitian. Compute eiθσx\ee^{\ii\theta\sigma_x}eiθσx​ for real θ\thetaθ using (0.5.47) rather than by summing a series.

Step 1, the spectrum. det⁡(σx−λI)=λ2−1=0\det(\sigma_x-\lambda I)=\lambda^{2}-1=0det(σx​−λI)=λ2−1=0, so λ=±1\lambda=\pm1λ=±1. The eigenvectors are the same ∣±⟩\ket{\pm}∣±⟩ as in Worked example 1. (Set E0=0E_0=0E0​=0 and Δ=1\Delta=1Δ=1 there and compare.) That gives the spectral decomposition

σx=(+1)P++(−1)P−=P+−P−. \sigma_x = (+1)P_{+} + (-1)P_{-} = P_{+}-P_{-}. σx​=(+1)P+​+(−1)P−​=P+​−P−​.

Step 2, apply the function. The operator in the exponent is θσx\theta\sigma_xθσx​, whose eigenvalues are ±θ\pm\theta±θ on the same eigenvectors. So with f(λ)=eiλf(\lambda)=\ee^{\ii\lambda}f(λ)=eiλ,

eiθσx=eiθP++e−iθP−. \ee^{\ii\theta\sigma_x} = \ee^{\ii\theta}P_{+} + \ee^{-\ii\theta}P_{-}. eiθσx​=eiθP+​+e−iθP−​.

Step 3, regroup using Euler. Write e±iθ=cos⁡θ±isin⁡θ\ee^{\pm\ii\theta}=\cos\theta\pm\ii\sin\thetae±iθ=cosθ±isinθ from Chapter 0.3 and collect the PPP's:

eiθσx=cos⁡θ (P++P−)+isin⁡θ (P+−P−)=cos⁡θ I+isin⁡θ σx, \begin{aligned} \ee^{\ii\theta\sigma_x} &= \cos\theta\,\big(P_{+}+P_{-}\big) + \ii\sin\theta\,\big(P_{+}-P_{-}\big)\\[4pt] &= \cos\theta\,I + \ii\sin\theta\,\sigma_x, \end{aligned} eiθσx​​=cosθ(P+​+P−​)+isinθ(P+​−P−​)=cosθI+isinθσx​,​

using completeness for the first bracket and Step 1 for the second. Written out as a matrix, that is

eiθσx=(cos⁡θisin⁡θisin⁡θcos⁡θ). \ee^{\ii\theta\sigma_x} = \begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta & \ii\sin\theta\\ \ii\sin\theta & \cos\theta\end{pmatrix}. eiθσx​=(cosθisinθ​isinθcosθ​).

What this is. Compare it with eiθ=cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ\ee^{\ii\theta}=\cos\theta+\ii\sin\thetaeiθ=cosθ+isinθ. The structure is identical, and this is Euler's formula with a matrix in the exponent. The reason it works is that σx2=I\sigma_x^{2}=Iσx2​=I, so σx\sigma_xσx​ plays the role that i\iii plays for numbers, except that it squares to +1+1+1 rather than −1-1−1. The eigenvalues ±1\pm1±1 are what carry the alternating signs. Any Hermitian MMM with M2=IM^{2}=IM2=I gives eiθM=cos⁡θ I+isin⁡θ M\ee^{\ii\theta M}=\cos\theta\,I+\ii\sin\theta\,MeiθM=cosθI+isinθM by the identical three steps.

Checks. Unitarity: (eiθσx)†=cos⁡θ I−isin⁡θ σx\big(\ee^{\ii\theta\sigma_x}\big)^{\dagger} = \cos\theta\,I - \ii\sin\theta\,\sigma_x(eiθσx​)†=cosθI−isinθσx​, and multiplying gives cos⁡2θ I+sin⁡2θ σx2=I\cos^{2}\theta\,I+\sin^{2}\theta\,\sigma_x^{2} = Icos2θI+sin2θσx2​=I ✓, as §7 promised. Determinant: cos⁡2θ−(isin⁡θ)2=cos⁡2θ+sin⁡2θ=1\cos^{2}\theta-(\ii\sin\theta)^{2}=\cos^{2}\theta+ \sin^{2}\theta=1cos2θ−(isinθ)2=cos2θ+sin2θ=1 ✓.

Where it goes. Unitary 2×22\times22×2 matrices of determinant 111 form the group SU(2)\mathrm{SU}(2)SU(2), and the operator above is a member of it. In Chapter 4.12, e−iθ n^⋅σ⃗/2\ee^{-\ii\theta\,\hat n\cdot\vec\sigma/2}e−iθn^⋅σ/2 is precisely the operator that rotates a spin-12\tfrac1221​ state about the axis n^\hat nn^ by angle θ\thetaθ. That is the same computation as this one, with a general unit vector in place of the xxx-direction. The factor of 12\tfrac1221​ in the exponent is why a spin must be turned through 720∘720^{\circ}720∘ to return to itself, and you can already see it coming: at θ=2π\theta=2\piθ=2π the formula above gives cos⁡π I=−I\cos\pi\,I=-IcosπI=−I, not III. Chapter 6.1 explains what kind of object does that.

Problem 1 · Gram–Schmidt, twice

(a) Apply (0.5.16) to the basis v1=(1,1,0)v_1=(1,1,0)v1​=(1,1,0), v2=(1,0,1)v_2=(1,0,1)v2​=(1,0,1), v3=(0,1,1)v_3=(0,1,1)v3​=(0,1,1) of R3\R^{3}R3 with the ordinary dot product. Verify the result is orthonormal.

w2=(1,0,1)−12⋅12(1,1,0)=(12,−12,1), w_2 = (1,0,1) - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1,0) = \left(\tfrac12,-\tfrac12,1\right), w2​=(1,0,1)−2​1​⋅2​1​(1,1,0)=(21​,−21​,1),

and normalising that vector gives the second basis element:

∥w2∥=14+14+1=32  ⟹  e2=16(1,−1,2). \left\lVert w_2\right\rVert = \sqrt{\tfrac14+\tfrac14+1} = \sqrt{\tfrac32} \;\Longrightarrow\; e_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}(1,-1,2). ∥w2​∥=41​+41​+1​=23​​⟹e2​=6​1​(1,−1,2).

w3=(0,1,1)−12(1,1,0)−16(1,−1,2)=(−23, 23, 23),∥w3∥=23, \begin{aligned} w_3 &= (0,1,1) - \tfrac12(1,1,0) - \tfrac16(1,-1,2)\\[3pt] &= \left(-\tfrac23,\ \tfrac23,\ \tfrac23\right), \qquad \left\lVert w_3\right\rVert=\tfrac{2}{\sqrt3}, \end{aligned} w3​​=(0,1,1)−21​(1,1,0)−61​(1,−1,2)=(−32​, 32​, 32​),∥w3​∥=3​2​,​

which normalises to

e3=13(−1,1,1). e_3 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}(-1,1,1). e3​=3​1​(−1,1,1).

Check. ⟨e1,e2⟩=112(1−1+0)=0\avg{e_1,e_2}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{12}}(1-1+0)=0⟨e1​,e2​⟩=12​1​(1−1+0)=0, and ⟨e1,e3⟩=16(−1+1+0)=0\avg{e_1,e_3}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}(-1+1+0)=0⟨e1​,e3​⟩=6​1​(−1+1+0)=0, and ⟨e2,e3⟩=118(−1−1+2)=0\avg{e_2,e_3}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{18}}(-1-1+2)=0⟨e2​,e3​⟩=18​1​(−1−1+2)=0. Each has norm 111 by construction. ✓

(b) ⟨1,1⟩=∫−11dx=2\avg{1,1}=\int_{-1}^{1}\dd x=2⟨1,1⟩=∫−11​dx=2, so e0=1/2e_0=1/\sqrt2e0​=1/2​.

So xxx is already orthogonal to the constants and nothing needs subtracting. With ⟨x,x⟩=∫−11x2dx=23\avg{x,x}=\int_{-1}^{1}x^{2}\dd x=\tfrac23⟨x,x⟩=∫−11​x2dx=32​, normalising gives

For x2x^{2}x2: ⟨e1,x2⟩=0\avg{e_1,x^{2}}=0⟨e1​,x2⟩=0 by oddness again, while ⟨e0,x2⟩=12⋅23\avg{e_0,x^{2}}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\tfrac23⟨e0​,x2⟩=2​1​⋅32​. Subtracting that one component,

w2=x2−12⋅23⋅12=x2−13, w_2 = x^{2} - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2} = x^{2}-\tfrac13, w2​=x2−2​1​⋅32​⋅2​1​=x2−31​,

and the norm of what is left is

∥w2∥2=∫−11 ⁣(x2−13)2dx=25−49+29=845, \left\lVert w_2\right\rVert^{2} = \int_{-1}^{1}\!\left(x^{2}-\tfrac13\right)^{2}\dd x = \tfrac25-\tfrac49+\tfrac29 = \tfrac{8}{45}, ∥w2​∥2=∫−11​(x2−31​)2dx=52​−94​+92​=458​,

so that dividing through by it gives

e2=458(x2−13)=52⋅3x2−12. e_2 = \sqrt{\tfrac{45}{8}}\left(x^{2}-\tfrac13\right) = \sqrt{\tfrac52}\cdot\tfrac{3x^{2}-1}{2}. e2​=845​​(x2−31​)=25​​⋅23x2−1​.

Those are the first three Legendre polynomials, normalised: P0=1P_0=1P0​=1, P1=xP_1=xP1​=x, P2=(3x2−1)/2P_2=(3x^{2}-1)/2P2​=(3x2−1)/2, each divided by 2/(2n+1)\sqrt{2/(2n+1)}2/(2n+1)​. They were not invented. They are what you get by running Gram–Schmidt on 1,x,x2,…1,x,x^{2},\dots1,x,x2,…, and there is nothing else they could have been. The identical procedure with a weight e−x2\ee^{-x^{2}}e−x2 on the whole line produces the Hermite polynomials, which are the quantum harmonic oscillator states of Chapter 4.8. The machinery does not care that the vectors are functions. That is the whole content of the abstraction, and it is what Chapter 4.3 will exploit.

Problem 2 · the spectrum of a unitary operator

Prove that every eigenvalue of a unitary operator has ∣λ∣=1\abs{\lambda}=1∣λ∣=1. Then interpret it: what does this say geometrically, and what would go wrong physically if it were false?

Solution

Let Uv=λvUv=\lambda vUv=λv with v≠0v\neq0v=0. Apply (0.5.32) with both arguments equal to vvv:

⟨v,v⟩=⟨Uv,Uv⟩=⟨λv,λv⟩=λˉλ⟨v,v⟩=∣λ∣2⟨v,v⟩. \avg{v,v} = \avg{Uv,Uv} = \avg{\lambda v,\lambda v} = \bar\lambda\lambda\avg{v,v} = \abs{\lambda}^{2}\avg{v,v}. ⟨v,v⟩=⟨Uv,Uv⟩=⟨λv,λv⟩=λˉλ⟨v,v⟩=∣λ∣2⟨v,v⟩.

Since v≠0v\neq0v=0, axiom (iii) gives ⟨v,v⟩>0\avg{v,v}\gt0⟨v,v⟩>0 and we may divide, leaving ∣λ∣2=1\abs{\lambda}^{2}=1∣λ∣2=1. So ∣λ∣=1\abs{\lambda}=1∣λ∣=1 and λ=eiφ\lambda=\ee^{\ii\varphi}λ=eiφ for some real φ\varphiφ.

Geometry. A unitary map preserves all lengths, so along any direction it preserves it must stretch by a factor of modulus one, which is to say not stretch at all but only rotate the phase. A unitary operator has no expanding or contracting directions anywhere. In its eigenbasis it is diag⁡(eiφ1,…,eiφn)\operatorname{diag}(\ee^{\ii\varphi_1},\dots,\ee^{\ii\varphi_n})diag(eiφ1​,…,eiφn​), a separate rotation on each of nnn perpendicular axes. Contrast a Hermitian operator, which in its eigenbasis is diag⁡(λ1,…,λn)\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)diag(λ1​,…,λn​) with the λi\lambda_iλi​ real: it only stretches and never rotates. The two classes are exactly complementary, which is the content of U=eiAU=\ee^{\ii A}U=eiA.

Physically. If some ∣λ∣>1\abs{\lambda}\gt1∣λ∣>1, a state along that eigenvector would grow in norm under repeated application of UUU. Since ∥ψ∥2\left\lVert \psi\right\rVert^{2}∥ψ∥2 is total probability, that state would end up with probability greater than one, meaning an outcome that occurs more often than always. If ∣λ∣<1\abs{\lambda}\lt1∣λ∣<1 the state would fade away and probability would leak out of the universe. Chapter 4.6's insistence on unitarity is exactly the demand that neither happens, and by the result above there is no third option, since unitary forces ∣λ∣=1\abs{\lambda}=1∣λ∣=1 automatically.

Problem 3 · symmetry is what makes the right angle

(a) Diagonalise S=(3113)S=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}S=(31​13​): find the eigenvalues, normalise the eigenvectors, and verify they are orthogonal.

(b) Now break the symmetry with N=(332123)N=\begin{pmatrix}3&\tfrac32\\[2pt]\tfrac12&3\end{pmatrix}N=(321​​23​3​), which has the same symmetric part. Find its eigenvalues and eigen-directions and compute the angle between them. Comment on what happened.

Solution

(a) det⁡(S−λI)=(3−λ)2−1=0\det(S-\lambda I)=(3-\lambda)^{2}-1=0det(S−λI)=(3−λ)2−1=0 gives 3−λ=±13-\lambda=\pm13−λ=±1, so λ=4\lambda=4λ=4 and λ=2\lambda=2λ=2. For λ=4\lambda=4λ=4: (−111−1)v=0\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}v=0(−11​1−1​)v=0 forces v1=v2v_1=v_2v1​=v2​, giving u1=12(1,1)u_{1}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1)u1​=2​1​(1,1), at 45∘45^{\circ}45∘. For λ=2\lambda=2λ=2: v1=−v2v_1=-v_2v1​=−v2​, giving u2=12(1,−1)u_{2}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,-1)u2​=2​1​(1,−1), at −45∘-45^{\circ}−45∘.

Orthogonality: u1⋅u2=12(1−1)=0u_1\cdot u_2=\tfrac12(1-1)=0u1​⋅u2​=21​(1−1)=0 ✓. The two eigen-directions are exactly 90∘90^{\circ}90∘ apart, as §6(b) guarantees for any real symmetric matrix with distinct eigenvalues.

(b) tr⁡N=6\operatorname{tr}N=6trN=6 and det⁡N=9−34=334\det N = 9-\tfrac34=\tfrac{33}{4}detN=9−43​=433​, so the quadratic formula gives

λ=6±36−332=3±32≈3.866, 2.134. \lambda = \frac{6\pm\sqrt{36-33}}{2} = 3\pm\frac{\sqrt3}{2} \approx 3.866,\ 2.134. λ=26±36−33​​=3±23​​≈3.866, 2.134.

Real, but that is luck rather than a theorem. The discriminant came out positive here and will not in general. For λ+=3+32\lambda_{+}=3+\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}λ+​=3+23​​, the first row of N−λ+IN-\lambda_{+}IN−λ+​I gives

−32v1+32v2=0  ⟹  v2=13v1, -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}v_1 + \tfrac32 v_2 = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; v_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}v_1, −23​​v1​+23​v2​=0⟹v2​=3​1​v1​,

a direction at arctan⁡(1/3)=30∘\arctan(1/\sqrt3)=30^{\circ}arctan(1/3​)=30∘. For λ−\lambda_{-}λ−​ the sign flips and the direction is at −30∘-30^{\circ}−30∘. Their dot product, with v±=(1,±1/3)v_{\pm}=(1,\pm 1/\sqrt3)v±​=(1,±1/3​), is 1−13=23≠01-\tfrac13=\tfrac23\neq01−31​=32​=0, so they are not perpendicular, and the angle between them follows from dividing by the two lengths:

cos⁡α=2/3(2/3)2=2/34/3=12  ⟹  α=60∘. \cos\alpha = \frac{2/3}{\left(2/\sqrt3\right)^{2}} = \frac{2/3}{4/3} = \frac12 \;\Longrightarrow\; \alpha = 60^{\circ}. cosα=(2/3​)22/3​=4/32/3​=21​⟹α=60∘.

Comment. The right angle is gone: 90∘90^{\circ}90∘ became 60∘60^{\circ}60∘. Nothing was done to the symmetric part of the matrix, since N=S+12(01−10)N = S + \tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}N=S+21​(0−1​10​) is an antisymmetric addition, and yet the eigen-directions tilted toward each other by 15∘15^{\circ}15∘ each. This is the figure of §5 with different numbers, and by (0.5.37) the eigenvalues would have gone complex once the antisymmetric coefficient exceeded half the eigenvalue gap of SSS, i.e. c=1c=1c=1. Orthogonality of eigenvectors is not a property of matrices. It is a property of Hermitian matrices, and it is lost the moment the hypothesis is.

Problem 4 · non-degenerate commuting operators share everything

Let AAA and BBB be Hermitian with [A,B]=0[A,B]=0[A,B]=0, and suppose AAA is non-degenerate: every eigenvalue of AAA has a one-dimensional eigenspace. Show that every eigenvector of AAA is automatically an eigenvector of BBB. Then explain why the general proof of §8 needed to be longer than this one.

Solution

Let Av=λvAv=\lambda vAv=λv with v≠0v\neq0v=0. We want to know where BBB sends vvv, so push BvBvBv through AAA and use AB=BAAB=BAAB=BA to move AAA inside:

A(Bv)=(AB)v=(BA)v=B(Av)=B(λv)=λ(Bv). A(Bv) = (AB)v = (BA)v = B(Av) = B(\lambda v) = \lambda(Bv). A(Bv)=(AB)v=(BA)v=B(Av)=B(λv)=λ(Bv).

So BvBvBv lies in the eigenspace EλE_\lambdaEλ​. By hypothesis EλE_\lambdaEλ​ is one-dimensional and contains vvv, so Eλ=span{v}E_\lambda = \mathrm{span}\{v\}Eλ​=span{v} and therefore Bv=μvBv=\mu vBv=μv for some scalar μ\muμ. Hence vvv is an eigenvector of BBB. (If Bv=0Bv=0Bv=0 then μ=0\mu=0μ=0, which is still an eigenvalue, since the zero vector is excluded as an eigenvector, not as an eigenvalue.) The eigenvectors of AAA already form an orthonormal basis, so that basis diagonalises BBB too. ■\blacksquare■

Why the general case is harder. The step "EλE_\lambdaEλ​ is one-dimensional, therefore BvBvBv is a multiple of vvv" is exactly what fails under degeneracy. If dim⁡Eλ=3\dim E_\lambda = 3dimEλ​=3, all we learn is that BBB maps that three-dimensional space into itself. The vector BvBvBv could be any vector in it, and a generic v∈Eλv\in E_\lambdav∈Eλ​ will not be an eigenvector of BBB. The repair is the whole content of the grind box in §8: BBB restricted to EλE_\lambdaEλ​ is still Hermitian, so the spectral theorem applies inside EλE_\lambdaEλ​ and selects the right basis there. Degeneracy does not break the theorem. It means AAA alone no longer specifies the basis and needs BBB's help to finish the job.

The physics of that last sentence, for later: a degenerate energy level is one where the Hamiltonian alone does not tell you which state you are in, and you must measure a second commuting observable to say. That is exactly why hydrogen states need three labels rather than one, and why "lifting a degeneracy" with a magnetic field, say, is such a common experimental move. Chapter 4.15.

The brick you just laid

You have the inner product from three axioms, with the conjugate forced by the demand that no non-zero vector have zero length, and every geometric notion rebuilt from it: length, distance, orthogonality, angle. You have Cauchy–Schwarz, proved by optimising a manifestly non-negative quantity, which is what makes "angle" definable at all. You have orthonormal bases, in which coordinates are inner products. You have Gram–Schmidt, which shows they always exist, and completeness, ∑i∣ei⟩⟨ei∣=I^\sum_i\ket{e_i}\bra{e_i}=\hat I∑i​∣ei​⟩⟨ei​∣=I^, in Dirac notation introduced where it is nothing but bookkeeping about rows and columns. You have orthogonal projection as the nearest-point map, and with it the fact that least-squares regression is a right angle and ANOVA is Pythagoras. You have the adjoint defined without reference to any basis, and shown to be the conjugate transpose in an orthonormal one. And you have the spectral theorem: a Hermitian operator has real eigenvalues, perpendicular eigenvectors, and a complete orthonormal eigenbasis, so that it dissolves into ∑iλi∣ei⟩⟨ei∣\sum_i\lambda_i\ket{e_i}\bra{e_i}∑i​λi​∣ei​⟩⟨ei​∣. Functions of operators, the Hermitian–unitary correspondence U=eiAU=\ee^{\ii A}U=eiA, and simultaneous diagonalisation of commuting operators all came out of it as corollaries.

Where this gets spent. Cauchy–Schwarz goes to Chapter 4.9, where it becomes the uncertainty principle with nothing added but interpretation. Orthonormal bases and completeness go to Chapter 4.2, for superposition and probability amplitudes, and to Chapter 0.9, where Fourier analysis turns out to be an orthonormal expansion in a function space and Parseval becomes conservation of energy across modes. Adjoint and Hermiticity go to Chapter 4.2, where "an observable is a Hermitian operator" is the one postulate that has to be made. The spectral theorem goes to Chapter 4.2 for the measurement postulates, which are these theorems renamed, to Chapters 4.7 and 4.8, where solving a system means diagonalising its Hamiltonian, to Chapter 0.8, where normal modes of coupled oscillators are eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix, and to every PCA you will ever run. eiA\ee^{\ii A}eiA goes to Chapter 4.6, where a Hermitian Hamiltonian generates unitary time evolution and probability is conserved as a matter of algebra, and to Chapter 6.1, where the same pairing becomes the Lie algebra of a Lie group. Commuting observables go to Chapters 4.9 and 4.11, where they become the complete set of quantum numbers that labels every state of every atom.

One thing remains outstanding, and it is worth naming so that you notice when it is paid. Every proof in this chapter used finite dimension: in the induction, in rank–nullity, in the interchange of sums, in the claim that an injective map is surjective. Quantum mechanics happens in infinite dimensions. Chapters 4.4 and 4.5 are where the bill comes due.
